claim: Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice encode a targeting construct following Hmmr exon 2.
source: We generated mice encoding a targeting construct following Hmmr exon 2, termed Hmmrtm1a(EUCOMM)Hmgu (hereafter Hmmrtm1a/tm1a, Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the generation of these mice with this specific genetic modification.

claim: HMMR expression was completely lost in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice.
source: Western blot analysis of lysates from tissues known to have elevated levels of HMMR expression (spleen and testes) (Line et al., 2002) using antibodies targeting the N-terminal peptide in HMMR revealed that HMMR expression was completely lost in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 1B demonstrates absence of HMMR protein in knockout mice.

claim: Adult Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice were rare.
source: Adult Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice were rare, and those Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice that did survive were smaller than their wild-type (WT) littermates (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation directly based on breeding outcomes.

claim: Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice that survived were smaller than their wild-type littermates.
source: Adult Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice were rare, and those Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice that did survive were smaller than their wild-type (WT) littermates (Figure 1C).
evidence: Figure 1C shows weight measurements demonstrating reduced body size in knockout mice.

claim: Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice exhibited atrophic seminiferous tubules.
source: Similar to the phenotypes seen in Hmmrm/m mice attributed to misoriented germ cell divisions (Li et al., 2016), we observed atrophic seminiferous tubules and an increase in apoptosis in the testes as indicated by TUNEL staining in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: Histological analysis shown in Figure 1D demonstrates atrophic tubules in knockout mice.

claim: Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice exhibited increased apoptosis in the testes.
source: Similar to the phenotypes seen in Hmmrm/m mice attributed to misoriented germ cell divisions (Li et al., 2016), we observed atrophic seminiferous tubules and an increase in apoptosis in the testes as indicated by TUNEL staining in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: TUNEL staining shown in Figure 1E demonstrates increased apoptosis in knockout testes.

claim: Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice were less fertile with fewer litters and fewer pups per litter.
source: Additionally, Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice were less fertile (fewer litters and fewer pups per litter) (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: Breeding data shown in Figures 1F and 1G demonstrate reduced fertility metrics.

claim: Few adult Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice survived despite no evidence of embryonic lethality at E14.5 and E18.5.
source: Few adult Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice survived despite no evidence of embryonic lethality at E14.5 and E18.5 (Figure 1H).
evidence: Figure 1H shows expected Mendelian ratios at embryonic stages but reduced survival at weaning.

claim: 12.5% of Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neonates were found dead within 3 hr of birth.
source: 12.5% of Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neonates were found dead within 3 hr of birth and 76.9% were found dead within the first 48 hr after birth (Figure 1I).
evidence: Survival analysis shown in Figure 1I demonstrates early neonatal mortality.

claim: 76.9% of Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neonates were found dead within the first 48 hr after birth.
source: 12.5% of Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neonates were found dead within 3 hr of birth and 76.9% were found dead within the first 48 hr after birth (Figure 1I).
evidence: Survival analysis shown in Figure 1I demonstrates high neonatal mortality within 48 hours.

claim: Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neonatal brains demonstrated morphological defects in overall structure and size.
source: Necropsy samples from Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neonates (P0-1) demonstrated morphological defects in the brain, including defects in overall structure and size (Figure 2A).
evidence: Figure 2A shows brain morphology differences between WT and knockout neonates.

claim: Three of nine Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neonatal brains measured two standard deviations smaller (microcephaly) than the mean brain size for age-matched WT littermates.
source: We found large variation in the size of Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neonatal brains with three of the nine measuring two standard deviations smaller (microcephaly) than the mean brain size for age-matched (P0-1) WT littermates (Figure 2B).
evidence: Quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2B demonstrate microcephaly in a subset of knockout brains.

claim: Three of nine Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neonatal brains measured two standard deviations larger (megalencephaly) than the mean brain size for age-matched WT littermates.
source: In addition, three of nine Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neonatal brains measured two standard deviations larger (megalencephaly) than the mean brain size for age-matched (P0-1) WT littermates, but these larger areas correlated with increases in the ventricle area in two of these three Hmmrtm1a/tm1a brains (Figure 2C).
evidence: Quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2C demonstrate megalencephaly in a subset of knockout brains.

claim: The larger brain areas in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice correlated with increases in ventricle area in two of three megalencephalic brains.
source: In addition, three of nine Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neonatal brains measured two standard deviations larger (megalencephaly) than the mean brain size for age-matched (P0-1) WT littermates, but these larger areas correlated with increases in the ventricle area in two of these three Hmmrtm1a/tm1a brains (Figure 2C).
evidence: Figure 2C shows correlation between brain size and ventricular area.

claim: The putative reduced cortical area in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a brains was not accompanied by increased levels of apoptosis at E18.5 or P0-1.
source: The putative reduced cortical area identified in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a relative to WT brains was not accompanied by increased levels of apoptosis, as measured by TUNEL staining, at either E18.5 or P0-1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: TUNEL staining quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A shows no difference in apoptosis levels.

claim: HMMR localized to spindle microtubules in dividing NP cells lining the ventricle surface in WT embryos.
source: In WT embryos, HMMR localized to spindle microtubules in dividing NP cells lining the ventricle surface (Figure 2D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 2D demonstrates HMMR localization to mitotic spindles.

claim: HMMR was absent from mitotic spindles in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a embryos.
source: In Hmmrtm1a/tm1a embryos, however, HMMR was absent from mitotic spindles (Figure 2D) and the axis for division was altered with an average angle of 24.8 ± 19.5 degrees (p<0.05; unpaired t-test) with only 38.5% or 66.6% of divisions oriented within 15 degrees or 30 degrees of the ventricular surface, respectively (χ2 test, p<0.001) (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 2D demonstrates absence of HMMR in knockout spindles.

claim: The average spindle angle in WT NP cells was 18.0 ± 19.5 degrees.
source: The angle of NP cell divisions measured during anaphase was strongly biased to be planar with the ventricle surface (<30 degrees off the axis of centrosomes lining the surface) with an average spindle angle of 18.0 ± 19.5 degrees (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2F demonstrate spindle orientation angles.

claim: In WT brains, 60.6% of divisions were oriented within 15 degrees of the ventricular surface.
source: In WT brains, 60.6% or 82.9% of divisions were oriented within 15 degrees or 30 degrees of the ventricular surface, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative analysis of spindle orientation angles in WT brains.

claim: In WT brains, 82.9% of divisions were oriented within 30 degrees of the ventricular surface.
source: In WT brains, 60.6% or 82.9% of divisions were oriented within 15 degrees or 30 degrees of the ventricular surface, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative analysis of spindle orientation angles in WT brains.

claim: The axis for division in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a embryos was altered with an average angle of 24.8 ± 19.5 degrees.
source: In Hmmrtm1a/tm1a embryos, however, HMMR was absent from mitotic spindles (Figure 2D) and the axis for division was altered with an average angle of 24.8 ± 19.5 degrees (p<0.05; unpaired t-test) with only 38.5% or 66.6% of divisions oriented within 15 degrees or 30 degrees of the ventricular surface, respectively (χ2 test, p<0.001) (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2F demonstrate altered spindle orientation in knockout cells.

claim: In Hmmrtm1a/tm1a embryos, only 38.5% of divisions were oriented within 15 degrees of the ventricular surface.
source: In Hmmrtm1a/tm1a embryos, however, HMMR was absent from mitotic spindles (Figure 2D) and the axis for division was altered with an average angle of 24.8 ± 19.5 degrees (p<0.05; unpaired t-test) with only 38.5% or 66.6% of divisions oriented within 15 degrees or 30 degrees of the ventricular surface, respectively (χ2 test, p<0.001) (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2F demonstrate altered spindle orientation in knockout cells.

claim: In Hmmrtm1a/tm1a embryos, only 66.6% of divisions were oriented within 30 degrees of the ventricular surface.
source: In Hmmrtm1a/tm1a embryos, however, HMMR was absent from mitotic spindles (Figure 2D) and the axis for division was altered with an average angle of 24.8 ± 19.5 degrees (p<0.05; unpaired t-test) with only 38.5% or 66.6% of divisions oriented within 15 degrees or 30 degrees of the ventricular surface, respectively (χ2 test, p<0.001) (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2F demonstrate altered spindle orientation in knockout cells.

claim: The degree of misorientation in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a NP cells compares to that observed in LGN-mutant NP cells.
source: The degree of misorientation observed in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a NP cells compares to that observed in LGN-mutant NP cells, which have 37.1% or 60% of divisions oriented within 15 degrees or 30 degrees of the ventricular surface, respectively (Konno et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript compares the observed phenotype to published data on LGN-mutant cells.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the number of mitotic Pax6+ radial glial cells at E14.5 in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a brains.
source: We also observed a significant reduction in the number of mitotic Pax6+ radial glial cells at E14.5 in the brains of Hmmrtm1a/tm1a embryos (Figure 2G–H) and a consistent, significant reduction in Tbr2+ intermediate progenitor cells in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a brains (Figure 2I–J).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 2H demonstrates reduced mitotic rate in knockout brains.

claim: There was a significant reduction in Tbr2+ intermediate progenitor cells in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a brains.
source: We also observed a significant reduction in the number of mitotic Pax6+ radial glial cells at E14.5 in the brains of Hmmrtm1a/tm1a embryos (Figure 2G–H) and a consistent, significant reduction in Tbr2+ intermediate progenitor cells in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a brains (Figure 2I–J).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 2J demonstrates reduced Tbr2+ cells in knockout brains.

claim: There was no significant difference between WT and Hmmrtm1a/tm1a brains in the levels of TUNEL-positive cells in the cortex.
source: However, we observed no significant difference between WT and Hmmrtm1a/tm1a brains in the levels of TUNEL-positive cells in the cortex, the localization of Par3 and ZO-1 in cells lining the ventricles, or the levels of centrosome amplification in dividing NP cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1A shows no difference in apoptosis levels.

claim: There was no significant difference between WT and Hmmrtm1a/tm1a brains in the localization of Par3 and ZO-1 in cells lining the ventricles.
source: However, we observed no significant difference between WT and Hmmrtm1a/tm1a brains in the levels of TUNEL-positive cells in the cortex, the localization of Par3 and ZO-1 in cells lining the ventricles, or the levels of centrosome amplification in dividing NP cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1B shows normal polarity marker localization.

claim: There was no significant difference between WT and Hmmrtm1a/tm1a brains in the levels of centrosome amplification in dividing NP cells.
source: However, we observed no significant difference between WT and Hmmrtm1a/tm1a brains in the levels of TUNEL-positive cells in the cortex, the localization of Par3 and ZO-1 in cells lining the ventricles, or the levels of centrosome amplification in dividing NP cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1C shows no centrosome amplification in knockout cells.

claim: The reduced cortical areas in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neonatal mice result from reduced production of intermediate progenitor cells corresponding with impaired planar spindle orientation during NP cell division and decreased mitotic rate of Pax6+ radial glial cells.
source: These data support the conclusion that the reduced cortical areas observed in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neonatal mice, which are less able to successfully transition to extrauterine life, result from the reduced production of intermediate progenitor cells that correspond with impaired planar spindle orientation during NP cell division and an overall decreased mitotic rate of Pax6+ radial glial cells.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes multiple observations to draw this conclusion.

claim: Hmmrtm1a/tm1a MEFs contained significantly higher levels of centrosome amplification.
source: Hmmrtm1a/tm1a MEFs contained significantly higher levels of centrosome amplification (defined as cells containing greater than two centrosomes, which were quantified using colocalization of pericentrin and γ–tubulin) (Figure 3B–C), and were less able to orient the cell division axis, measured at anaphase relative to their long cell axis in interphase (Figure 3A,D–E).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 3C demonstrates increased centrosome amplification in knockout MEFs.

claim: Hmmrtm1a/tm1a MEFs were less able to orient the cell division axis.
source: Hmmrtm1a/tm1a MEFs contained significantly higher levels of centrosome amplification (defined as cells containing greater than two centrosomes, which were quantified using colocalization of pericentrin and γ–tubulin) (Figure 3B–C), and were less able to orient the cell division axis, measured at anaphase relative to their long cell axis in interphase (Figure 3A,D–E).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 3E demonstrates spindle orientation defects in knockout MEFs.

claim: Hmmrtm1a/tm1a MEF progeny cells were more likely to display indications of genome instability, including increases in the frequency of mitotic death, binucleated progeny and micronuclei.
source: In addition, Hmmrtm1a/tm1a MEF progeny cells were more likely to display indications of genome instability, including increases in the frequency of mitotic death, binucleated progeny and micronuclei (Figure 3F).
evidence: Figure 3F shows increased frequency of mitotic defects in knockout MEFs.

claim: The width to long axis ratio of the cell did not differ between WT or Hmmrtm1a/tm1a MEFs.
source: To ensure that the observed spindle orientation defects were not due to changes in cell shape that may accompany the loss of HMMR, we confirmed that the width to long axis ratio of the cell did not differ between WT or Hmmrtm1a/tm1a MEFs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1A shows no difference in cell elongation between WT and knockout MEFs.

claim: The transduction of HMMRFL or HMMR1-679 recovered the axis of cell division in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a MEFs.
source: The transduction of HMMRFL or HMMR1-679, gene products that are known to locate at centrosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)(Maxwell et al., 2003), recovered the axis of cell division (Figure 3E).
evidence: Figure 3E shows rescue of spindle orientation defects with HMMRFL or HMMR1-679 expression.

claim: The expression of HMMR1-623 failed to rescue the axis of cell division in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a MEFs.
source: However, the expression of HMMR1-623 failed to rescue the axis of cell division (Figure 3E), implicating the centrosome targeting bZip motif (amino acids 624–679) as an essential domain for the orientation of cell division.
evidence: Figure 3E shows failure to rescue spindle orientation with HMMR1-623 expression.

claim: The centrosome targeting bZip motif (amino acids 624–679) is an essential domain for the orientation of cell division.
source: However, the expression of HMMR1-623 failed to rescue the axis of cell division (Figure 3E), implicating the centrosome targeting bZip motif (amino acids 624–679) as an essential domain for the orientation of cell division.
evidence: The rescue experiments demonstrate the requirement of this domain for spindle orientation.

claim: In control-treated cells with an off-center mitotic spindle, DHC-GFP was asymmetrically localized to the far polar region of the cortex and absent from the cortex near the proximal pole leading to the correction of spindle position.
source: Immediately prior to anaphase in control-treated cells with an off-center mitotic spindle, DHC-GFP was asymmetrically localized to the far polar region of the cortex and absent from the cortex near the proximal pole leading to the correction of spindle position (Figure 4A, Video 1) as described previously (Kiyomitsu and Cheeseman, 2012).
evidence: Live imaging shown in Figure 4A and Video 1 demonstrates asymmetric DHC-GFP localization in control cells.

claim: In HMMR-silenced cells with an off-center mitotic spindle, DHC-GFP remained on the polar cortex and its retention on the cortex predicted the direction of spindle rotation.
source: In HMMR-silenced cells with an off-center mitotic spindle, however, DHC-GFP remained on the polar cortex and its retention on the cortex predicted the direction of spindle rotation (Figure 4A, Video 2).
evidence: Live imaging shown in Figure 4A and Video 2 demonstrates retention of DHC-GFP in HMMR-silenced cells.

claim: Overall DHC-GFP recruitment to crescents was not significantly different between scrambled control-treated and HMMR-silenced cells.
source: We also measured the intensity of DHC-GFP recruited to the cortex relative to the cytoplasmic intensity and determined that overall DHC-GFP recruitment to crescents was not significantly different between scrambled control-treated and HMMR-silenced cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A shows no difference in overall DHC-GFP recruitment.

claim: The spindle was maintained in an off-centered position in HMMR-silenced cells.
source: In addition, the spindle was maintained in an off-centered position in HMMR-silenced cells as determined by the ratio of the distance between the cortex and the location of chromosomes in anaphase cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 4B demonstrates off-center spindle position in HMMR-silenced cells.

claim: A prolonged period of spindle rotation was frequently observed in HMMR-silenced HeLa cells expressing DHC-GFP.
source: A prolonged period of spindle rotation was frequently observed in HMMR-silenced HeLa cells expressing DHC-GFP (Figure 4C) and, as seen in separate experiments, in HMMR-silenced HeLa cells expressing mCherry histone H2B, eGFP-TUBA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C; Videos 3–4).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 4C and live imaging in Videos 3-4 demonstrate spindle rotation in HMMR-silenced cells.

claim: NuMA was retained at the proximal polar cortex in HMMR-silenced mitotic cells with an off-center metaphase spindle.
source: However, NuMA was retained at the proximal polar cortex and the consequent ratio of intensities was significantly dampened in HMMR-silenced mitotic cells with an off-center metaphase spindle (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and quantification shown in Figures 4D-E demonstrate NuMA retention in HMMR-silenced cells.

claim: When the metaphase spindle was centered, the asymmetric cortical localization of NuMA and DHC-GFP was indistinguishable in control-treated and HMMR-silenced cells.
source: Yet, when the metaphase spindle was centered, the asymmetric cortical localization of NuMA and DHC-GFP was indistinguishable in control-treated and HMMR-silenced cells (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and quantification shown in Figures 4F-G demonstrate normal NuMA localization in centered spindles.

claim: HMMR is dispensable for the loss of NuMA and DHC-GFP at the midzone cortical region.
source: Our data indicate HMMR is dispensable for the loss of NuMA and DHC-GFP at the midzone cortical region, which is established by Ran-GTP gradient generated at chromosomes (Kiyomitsu and Cheeseman, 2012), but HMMR is needed for a centrosome-localized positioning pathway that strips NuMA and DHC-GFP when the pole is brought proximal to the cortex.
evidence: The data from Figures 4F-G support this conclusion about HMMR function.

claim: HMMR is needed for a centrosome-localized positioning pathway that strips NuMA and DHC-GFP when the pole is brought proximal to the cortex.
source: Our data indicate HMMR is dispensable for the loss of NuMA and DHC-GFP at the midzone cortical region, which is established by Ran-GTP gradient generated at chromosomes (Kiyomitsu and Cheeseman, 2012), but HMMR is needed for a centrosome-localized positioning pathway that strips NuMA and DHC-GFP when the pole is brought proximal to the cortex.
evidence: The data from Figures 4D-E support this conclusion about HMMR function.

claim: In HMMR-silenced lysates, the abundance of subunits for dynein (DHC, DIC, and DYNLL1) and dynactin (p150glued) were unchanged.
source: In HMMR-silenced lysates, relative to control-treated lysates, the abundance of subunits for dynein (DHC, dynein intermediate chain (DIC), and DYNLL1) and dynactin (p150glued) were unchanged (Figure 5A).
evidence: Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5A demonstrates unchanged protein levels.

claim: The level of co-precipitated DYNLL1 was reduced in HMMR-silenced lysates.
source: While the amount of DHC-GFP precipitated and the levels of DIC co-precipitated with DHC-GFP remained unaffected, the level of co-precipitated DYNLL1 was reduced in HMMR-silenced lysates (Figure 5A).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 5A demonstrates reduced DYNLL1 interaction with DHC-GFP.

claim: A corresponding reduction in p150glued co-precipitated with DHC-GFP was observed in HMMR-silenced lysates.
source: Moreover, a corresponding reduction in p150glued co-precipitated with DHC-GFP was also observed in HMMR-silenced lysates (Figure 5A).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 5A demonstrates reduced p150glued interaction with DHC-GFP.

claim: Both FLAG-DYNLL1 and CHICA were retained at spindle poles, although absent from spindle fibers, in HMMR-silenced cells.
source: We also noted that both FLAG-DYNLL1 and CHICA were retained at spindle poles, although absent from spindle fibers, in HMMR-silenced cells (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence shown in Figures 5B-C demonstrates localization of DYNLL1 and CHICA in HMMR-silenced cells.

claim: HMMR is dispensable for the spindle pole localization of CHICA and DYNLL1.
source: Therefore, HMMR appears dispensable for the spindle pole localization of CHICA and DYNLL1 and HMMR promotes, rather than restricts, the incorporation of p150glued into DHC complexes.
evidence: The data from Figures 5B-C support this conclusion.

claim: HMMR promotes, rather than restricts, the incorporation of p150glued into DHC complexes.
source: Therefore, HMMR appears dispensable for the spindle pole localization of CHICA and DYNLL1 and HMMR promotes, rather than restricts, the incorporation of p150glued into DHC complexes.
evidence: The data from Figure 5A support this conclusion.

claim: A significant reduction in the fluorescence intensity of pPLK1 at spindle poles was observed in HMMR-silenced mitotic cells.
source: In HMMR-silenced mitotic cells, we observed a significant reduction in the fluorescence intensity of pPLK1 at spindle poles (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and quantification shown in Figures 5D-E demonstrate reduced pPLK1 levels.

claim: A significant decrease in the number of EB1-positive microtubule plus ends contacting the cortex was observed in HMMR-silenced or BI2536-treated mitotic cells.
source: Consistent with a putative reduction in PLK1 activity at spindle poles, we observed a significant decrease in the number of EB1-positive microtubule plus ends contacting the cortex in HMMR-silenced or BI2536-treated mitotic cells (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and quantification shown in Figures 5F-G demonstrate reduced astral microtubule contacts.

claim: In control-treated cells, NuMA was uniformly absent from the cortex.
source: In control-treated cells, NuMA was uniformly absent from the cortex, while NuMA was largely retained in HMMR-silenced cells with the exception of a discreet loss in the inner region directly proximal to the pole (Figure 5H–I).
evidence: Immunofluorescence shown in Figure 5H demonstrates NuMA localization in control cells.

claim: NuMA was largely retained in HMMR-silenced cells with the exception of a discreet loss in the inner region directly proximal to the pole.
source: In control-treated cells, NuMA was uniformly absent from the cortex, while NuMA was largely retained in HMMR-silenced cells with the exception of a discreet loss in the inner region directly proximal to the pole (Figure 5H–I).
evidence: Immunofluorescence shown in Figure 5H demonstrates NuMA localization in HMMR-silenced cells.

claim: In mitotic cells treated with BI2536, the localization of NuMA mirrored that observed in HMMR-silenced cells and was not additively altered in dual inhibited cells.
source: In mitotic cells treated with BI2536, the localization of NuMA mirrored that observed in HMMR-silenced cells and was not additively altered in dual inhibited cells (Figure 5H–I) consistent with a requirement for PLK1 and HMMR in a shared positioning pathway.
evidence: Immunofluorescence and quantification shown in Figures 5H-I demonstrate similar NuMA localization with PLK1 inhibition and HMMR silencing.

claim: PLK1 and HMMR are required in a shared positioning pathway.
source: In mitotic cells treated with BI2536, the localization of NuMA mirrored that observed in HMMR-silenced cells and was not additively altered in dual inhibited cells (Figure 5H–I) consistent with a requirement for PLK1 and HMMR in a shared positioning pathway.
evidence: The lack of additive effect suggests HMMR and PLK1 function in the same pathway.

claim: Astral microtubule density is dampened in HMMR-silenced mitotic cells in a PLK1-dependent manner.
source: Thus, our data supports the conclusion that astral microtubule density is dampened in HMMR-silenced mitotic cells in a PLK1-dependent manner, which disturbs the spindle pole-localized positioning pathway and results in spindle rotation due to the retention of NuMA-DHC complexes at the proximal cortex.
evidence: The data from Figures 5F-G and 5H-I support this conclusion.

claim: PLK1 phosphorylates HMMR at threonine 703.
source: As PLK1 phosphorylates HMMR at threonine 703 (pHMMR) (Nousiainen et al., 2006), we used mass spectrometry to identify proteins that are co-precipitated with antibodies targeting pHMMR as a means to discover putative pathways through which centrosome-localized HMMR may regulate spindle position.
evidence: The manuscript cites published data identifying this phosphorylation site.

claim: FAM83D/CHICA and DYNLL1 were identified in pHMMR immunoprecipitates.
source: In pHMMR immunoprecipitates from mitotic or G2-phase synchronized HeLa cell lysates, we identified a number of actin-, myosin-, and dynein-binding proteins (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Figure 6—source data 1), including known interactors FAM83D/CHICA and DYNLL1 (Dunsch et al., 2012).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 identifies these proteins.

claim: ARHGAP17, RACGAP1, and RanBP2 were uniquely co-precipitated with pHMMR antibodies.
source: We filtered out proteins that were also co-precipitated with antibodies targeting a non-phosphorylated N-terminal peptide in HMMR (unpublished results) and found that proteins related to small GTPases, such as ARHGAP17, RACGAP1, and RanBP2, were uniquely co-precipitated with pHMMR antibodies (Figure 6A).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6A identifies these proteins as unique to pHMMR immunoprecipitates.

claim: The pHMMR-RanBP2 interaction was confirmed by western blot analysis.
source: As Ran regulates cortical LGN-NuMA-dynein localization during mitosis (Kiyomitsu and Cheeseman, 2012), we focused on the putative pHMMR-RanBP2 interaction and confirmed this interaction by western blot analysis (Figure 6B).
evidence: Western blot shown in Figure 6B confirms the interaction.

claim: In HMMR-silenced cell lysates, the level of Ran-GTP precipitated was slightly reduced relative to scrambled control-treated cell lysates.
source: In HMMR-silenced cell lysates, the level of Ran-GTP precipitated was slightly reduced relative to scrambled control-treated cell lysates (Figure 6C).
evidence: Ran activity assay shown in Figure 6C demonstrates reduced Ran-GTP levels.

claim: HMMR was co-precipitated when lysates were pretreated with GTPγS.
source: When we confirmed the knockdown efficacy of HMMR in these experiments, we noted that HMMR was also co-precipitated when lysates were pretreated with GTPγS suggesting HMMR may interact specifically with Ran-GTP, which is greatly increased by GTPγS treatment.
evidence: The observation from the Ran activity assay suggests this interaction.

claim: The level of Ran co-precipitated with HMMR was increased in a GTPγS dose-dependent manner.
source: While the levels of precipitated HMMR remained constant, we found that the level of Ran co-precipitated with HMMR was increased in a GTPγS dose-dependent manner (Figure 6D).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 6D demonstrates dose-dependent interaction.

claim: HMMR interacts with Ran-GTPγS in cell lysates.
source: Thus, HMMR interacts with Ran-GTPγS in cell lysates.
evidence: The data from Figure 6D support this conclusion.

claim: A fraction of RanCA colocalized with the spindle pole demarked by γ-tubulin in scrambled siRNA-treated cells.
source: In scrambled siRNA-treated cells, a fraction of RanCA colocalized with the spindle pole demarked by γ-tubulin (Figure 6E), consistent with the identification of Ran in the centrosome proteome (Andersen et al., 2003).
evidence: Immunofluorescence shown in Figure 6E demonstrates RanCA localization at centrosomes.

claim: The fraction of RanCA that colocalized with γ-tubulin was significantly reduced in HMMR-silenced cells.
source: However, the fraction of RanCA that colocalized with γ-tubulin, as measured by the ratio of intensities for RanCA and γ-tubulin, was significantly reduced in HMMR-silenced cells (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and quantification shown in Figures 6E-F demonstrate reduced RanCA at centrosomes.

claim: Inhibition of PLK1 activity reduced the fraction of RanCA that colocalized with γ-tubulin.
source: Similarly, inhibition of PLK1 activity, through treatment with a small-molecule inhibitor BI2536, also reduced the fraction of RanCA that colocalized with γ-tubulin (Figure 6G–H).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and quantification shown in Figures 6G-H demonstrate reduced RanCA at centrosomes with PLK1 inhibition.

claim: Reducing PLK1 activity or silencing HMMR reduces the localization of constitutively active Ran at mitotic centrosomes.
source: This data shows that reducing PLK1 activity or silencing HMMR reduces the localization of constitutively active Ran at mitotic centrosomes and suggests the phosphorylation of HMMR (pHMMR) by PLK1 may promote pHMMR-RanBP2-Ran-GTP complexes at spindle poles.
evidence: The data from Figures 6E-H support this conclusion.

claim: The phosphorylation of HMMR (pHMMR) by PLK1 may promote pHMMR-RanBP2-Ran-GTP complexes at spindle poles.
source: This data shows that reducing PLK1 activity or silencing HMMR reduces the localization of constitutively active Ran at mitotic centrosomes and suggests the phosphorylation of HMMR (pHMMR) by PLK1 may promote pHMMR-RanBP2-Ran-GTP complexes at spindle poles.
evidence: The data from Figures 6B and 6E-H support this speculation.

claim: A decrease in the immunofluorescence intensity detected for endogenous Ran colocalized with pericentrin was observed in HMMR-silenced SHSY5Y cells compared to control-treated cells.
source: In HMMR-silenced cells compared to control-treated cells, we observed a decrease in the immunofluorescence intensity detected for endogenous Ran colocalized with pericentrin, a centrosome marker (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and quantification shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-C demonstrate reduced Ran at centrosomes.

claim: Spindles in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neural progenitors were less centered compared to spindles within wild-type progenitor cells.
source: When compared to spindles within wild-type progenitor cells, spindles in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neural progenitors were less centered (a/b measurement) and significantly shorter (c measurement) (Figure 7B).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 7B demonstrates spindle positioning defects.

claim: Spindles in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neural progenitors were significantly shorter compared to spindles within wild-type progenitor cells.
source: When compared to spindles within wild-type progenitor cells, spindles in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neural progenitors were less centered (a/b measurement) and significantly shorter (c measurement) (Figure 7B).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 7B demonstrates reduced spindle length.

claim: The density of spindle fibers was significantly lower in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neural progenitors than those in WT cells.
source: Additionally, the density of spindle fibers, as measured by the intensity of beta-tubulin fluorescence, was significantly lower in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a neural progenitors than those in WT cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 7C demonstrates reduced spindle density.

claim: A fraction of endogenous Ran colocalized with γ-tubulin in neural progenitor cells.
source: Similar to our observations in HMMR-silenced HeLa or SH-SY5Y cells, we found a fraction of endogenous Ran, as measured by immunofluorescence, colocalized with a centrosome marker (γ-tubulin, Figure 7D); this fraction of Ran, as measured by the ratio of intensities for Ran and γ-tubulin, was significantly reduced in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a relative to WT neural progenitors (Figure 7E).
evidence: Immunofluorescence shown in Figure 7D demonstrates Ran localization at centrosomes.

claim: The fraction of Ran colocalized with γ-tubulin was significantly reduced in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a relative to WT neural progenitors.
source: Similar to our observations in HMMR-silenced HeLa or SH-SY5Y cells, we found a fraction of endogenous Ran, as measured by immunofluorescence, colocalized with a centrosome marker (γ-tubulin, Figure 7D); this fraction of Ran, as measured by the ratio of intensities for Ran and γ-tubulin, was significantly reduced in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a relative to WT neural progenitors (Figure 7E).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 7E demonstrates reduced Ran at centrosomes in knockout cells.

claim: HMMR supports PLK1 activity at the centrosome.
source: Our in vitro data support a model where HMMR supports PLK1 activity at the centrosome, which stabilizes astral microtubules and through the phosphorylation of HMMR localizes Ran to mitotic spindle poles.
evidence: The data from Figures 5D-E and 6E-H support this model.

claim: PLK1 activity stabilizes astral microtubules.
source: Our in vitro data support a model where HMMR supports PLK1 activity at the centrosome, which stabilizes astral microtubules and through the phosphorylation of HMMR localizes Ran to mitotic spindle poles.
evidence: The data from Figures 5F-G support this model.

claim: Through the phosphorylation of HMMR, PLK1 localizes Ran to mitotic spindle poles.
source: Our in vitro data support a model where HMMR supports PLK1 activity at the centrosome, which stabilizes astral microtubules and through the phosphorylation of HMMR localizes Ran to mitotic spindle poles.
evidence: The data from Figures 6B and 6E-H support this model.

claim: PLK1-dependent spindle pole positioning processes are critical to reduce cortical localization of NuMA-DHC in off-center spindles and prevent spindle rotation.
source: These PLK1-dependent spindle pole positioning processes are critical to reduce cortical localization of NuMA-DHC in off-center spindles and prevent spindle rotation (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The data from Figures 4 and 5 support this conclusion.

claim: In induced tet-HMMR cells, metaphase spindles were more frequently off-center.
source: In subconfluent cultures of induced tet-HMMR cells, metaphase spindles were more frequently off-center (Figure 8B).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 8B demonstrates increased off-center spindles with HMMR overexpression.

claim: In HeLa cells, RanWT was cytoplasmic, RanCA localized to the mitotic spindle, and RanDN localized to the chromosomes.
source: In HeLa cells, these constructs localized as previously reported (Hutchins et al., 2009): RanWT was cytoplasmic, RanCA localized to the mitotic spindle, and RanDN localized to the chromosomes (Figure 8C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence shown in Figure 8C demonstrates Ran construct localization.

claim: In induced tet-HMMR cells, RanWT localized to the spindle similar to that of RanCA.
source: In induced tet-HMMR cells, however, RanWT localized to the spindle similar to that of RanCA (Figure 8C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence shown in Figure 8C demonstrates altered RanWT localization with HMMR overexpression.

claim: Induction of GFP-HMMR expression caused NuMA to be lost entirely from the cortex.
source: Induction of GFP-HMMR expression also caused NuMA to be lost entirely from the cortex (Figure 8D–E).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and quantification shown in Figures 8D-E demonstrate loss of cortical NuMA.

claim: A similar effect on cortical NuMA localization was observed in HeLa cells overexpressing RanCA.
source: We observed a similar effect on cortical NuMA localization in HeLa cells overexpressing RanCA (Figure 8F–G).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and quantification shown in Figures 8F-G demonstrate loss of cortical NuMA with RanCA overexpression.

claim: Expression of GFP-HMMR induces defects in the spindle positioning pathway that are consistent with an ectopic localization of Ran-GTP on mitotic spindles.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that expression of GFP-HMMR induces defects in the spindle positioning pathway that are consistent with an ectopic localization of Ran-GTP on mitotic spindles (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The data from Figures 8C-G support this conclusion.

claim: Hmmr−/− animals exhibited fertility defects.
source: An initial murine model, termed Hmmr−/−, was generated by targeted disruption at exon 8 (Tolg et al., 2003) while an alternative model, termed Hmmrm/m, was generated by targeted disruption at exon 10 (Li et al., 2015); thus, truncated N-terminal Hmmr transcript or protein is expressed in both of these published Hmmr models. Hmmr−/− animals exhibited fertility defects (Tolg et al., 2003), while Hmmrm/m mice demonstrated deficient spindle orientation during gametogenesis (Li et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on Hmmr−/− mice.

claim: Hmmrm/m mice demonstrated deficient spindle orientation during gametogenesis.
source: An initial murine model, termed Hmmr−/−, was generated by targeted disruption at exon 8 (Tolg et al., 2003) while an alternative model, termed Hmmrm/m, was generated by targeted disruption at exon 10 (Li et al., 2015); thus, truncated N-terminal Hmmr transcript or protein is expressed in both of these published Hmmr models. Hmmr−/− animals exhibited fertility defects (Tolg et al., 2003), while Hmmrm/m mice demonstrated deficient spindle orientation during gametogenesis (Li et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on Hmmrm/m mice.

claim: Hmmrm/m and Hmmr−/− animals are both viable and phenotypically normal.
source: However, Hmmrm/m and Hmmr−/− animals are both viable and phenotypically normal.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation to contrast with Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice.

claim: Microcephaly and enlarged ventricles can arise from defects in spindle orientation and planar cell division within the progenitor population.
source: We observed in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice previously unseen neural defects such as enlarged ventricles and microcephaly; both of these congenital conditions can arise from defects in spindle orientation and planar cell division within the progenitor population (Lancaster and Knoblich, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites published knowledge about the relationship between spindle orientation and brain development.

claim: Misoriented division planes were identified in apical neuroprogenitors and postnatal granule cell precursors during brain development of Hmmrm/m mice.
source: A recent study identified misoriented division planes in apical neuroprogenitors and postnatal granule cell precursors, without changes to the cell division rate, during brain development of Hmmrm/m mice expressing truncated N-terminal Hmmr protein (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on Hmmrm/m mice.

claim: Transient megalencephaly was observed in Hmmrm/m brains during the neuronal differentiation period, up to PND7 but normalized by PND14.
source: Transient megalencephaly was observed in Hmmrm/m brains during the neuronal differentiation period, up to PND7 but normalized by PND14, and attributed to misoriented divisions in apical neuroprogenitors leading to an increased number of Tbr+ intermediate progenitors contributing to cerebral cortex enlargement (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on Hmmrm/m mice.

claim: The different neural phenotypes between Hmmrm/m and Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice imply the expression of truncated N-terminal Hmmr protein retains critical functions needed for neural development and neonatal survival.
source: The different neural phenotypes between Hmmrm/m and Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice imply the expression of truncated N-terminal Hmmr protein retains critical functions needed for neural development and neonatal survival.
evidence: The manuscript draws this inference from comparing the two mouse models.

claim: The microtubule-binding domain of HMMR has been shown to be important for neural development in Xenopus.
source: In support of this, the microtubule-binding domain of HMMR (Assmann et al., 1999; Maxwell et al., 2003) has recently been shown to be important for neural development in Xenopus (Prager et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on HMMR function in Xenopus.

claim: Microinjection of morpholinos targeting Hmmr in Xenopus laevis embryos resulted in gross alterations in forebrain morphogenesis and anterior neural tube closure.
source: Microinjection of morpholinos targeting Hmmr in Xenopus laevis embryos resulted in gross alterations in forebrain morphogenesis and anterior neural tube closure and these defects were rescued by the expression a truncated HMMR construct that preserved the microtubule-binding domain (Prager et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on HMMR function in Xenopus.

claim: Directed smooth muscle cell migration following balloon catheter injury in rats is reliant upon HMMR.
source: Directed smooth muscle cell migration following balloon catheter injury in rats is reliant upon HMMR (Silverman-Gavrila et al., 2011), and HMMR is expressed in cells within the SVZ and rostral migratory stream in the adult mouse brain, where neural progenitor cells persist throughout life (Lindwall et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on HMMR function in cell migration.

claim: HMMR is expressed in cells within the SVZ and rostral migratory stream in the adult mouse brain.
source: Directed smooth muscle cell migration following balloon catheter injury in rats is reliant upon HMMR (Silverman-Gavrila et al., 2011), and HMMR is expressed in cells within the SVZ and rostral migratory stream in the adult mouse brain, where neural progenitor cells persist throughout life (Lindwall et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on HMMR expression in the adult brain.

claim: Hmmr/HMMR expression was restricted to apical-positioned, cyclin B1-positive rosette-neural stem cells.
source: When we derived neural rosette-like structures from a mouse mouse HmmrBB0166/+ ESC line (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E), in which β-geo is inserted following Hmmr exon 7 on one allele, or from WT ESCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F), we found Hmmr/HMMR expression was restricted to apical-positioned, cyclin B1-positive rosette-neural stem cells (r-NSCs); moreover, spindle position was disturbed in apical-positioned r-NSCs derived from HmmrBB0166/+ mESCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: Data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F demonstrates cell cycle-restricted HMMR expression.

claim: Spindle position was disturbed in apical-positioned r-NSCs derived from HmmrBB0166/+ mESCs.
source: When we derived neural rosette-like structures from a mouse mouse HmmrBB0166/+ ESC line (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E), in which β-geo is inserted following Hmmr exon 7 on one allele, or from WT ESCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F), we found Hmmr/HMMR expression was restricted to apical-positioned, cyclin B1-positive rosette-neural stem cells (r-NSCs); moreover, spindle position was disturbed in apical-positioned r-NSCs derived from HmmrBB0166/+ mESCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: Data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G-H demonstrates spindle positioning defects.

claim: Hmmr shows cell cycle-restricted expression in G2 phase and mitotic cells during the process of neural differentiation.
source: Thus, Hmmr shows cell cycle-restricted expression in G2 phase and mitotic cells during the process of neural differentiation, and our data are consistent with the defects we observed in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice being attributed to alterations in neural progenitor expansion and differentiation as determined by changes to the control of spindle orientation and cell division.
evidence: The data from Figure 7—figure supplement 1F support this conclusion.

claim: The defects observed in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice are attributed to alterations in neural progenitor expansion and differentiation as determined by changes to the control of spindle orientation and cell division.
source: Thus, Hmmr shows cell cycle-restricted expression in G2 phase and mitotic cells during the process of neural differentiation, and our data are consistent with the defects we observed in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice being attributed to alterations in neural progenitor expansion and differentiation as determined by changes to the control of spindle orientation and cell division.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes multiple observations to draw this conclusion.

claim: HMMR is critical to spindle positioning.
source: Moreover, in HeLa cells, HMMR is critical to spindle positioning (Dunsch et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on HMMR function in HeLa cells.

claim: An elevated occurrence of supernumerary centrosomes results in embryonic lethality.
source: An elevated occurrence of supernumerary centrosomes, as induced for example through overexpression of PLK4, results in embryonic lethality (Vitre et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on the effects of centrosome amplification.

claim: A loss of control of the cell division axis has been consistently observed in HMMR-silenced HeLa cells.
source: A loss of control of the cell division axis, however, has been consistently observed in HMMR-silenced HeLa cells (Dunsch et al., 2012) and, as described here, in r-NSCs derived from HmmrBB1066/+ mESCs, Hmmrtm1a/tm1a MEFs, and neural progenitor cells lining the SVZ in brains isolated from Hmmrtm1a/tm1a mice.
evidence: The manuscript cites published data and presents new data on spindle orientation defects.

claim: The intrinsic spindle positioning pathway regulates components of the dynein motor complex on the cortex to generate forces that center spindles.
source: The intrinsic spindle positioning pathway regulates components of the dynein motor complex on the cortex to generate forces that center spindles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the spindle positioning pathway.

claim: The PLK1 gradient at both centrosomes and kinetochores is essential in regulating the spindle positioning pathway.
source: It is well recognized that the PLK1 gradient at both centrosomes and kinetochores is essential in regulating the spindle positioning pathway (Kiyomitsu and Cheeseman, 2012; Tame et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites published knowledge about PLK1 function.

claim: HMMR is a critical component of a PLK1-dependent positioning pathway.
source: Here, we find HMMR is a critical component of a PLK1-dependent positioning pathway, which contrasts with the findings of a prior report that predicts HMMR-CHICA-DYNLL1 play a PLK1-independent role that regulates the composition of cortical dynein complexes (Dunsch et al., 2012).
evidence: The data from Figures 5 and 6 support this conclusion.

claim: HMMR acts downstream from Ran-GTP to localize TPX2.
source: HMMR acts downstream from Ran-GTP to localize TPX2 (Groen et al., 2004; Joukov et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2014; Scrofani et al., 2015), which relies upon a carboxy-terminal bZip motif in HMMR (Maxwell et al., 2003) and enables the activation of Aurora A by TPX2 (Chen et al., 2014) (Scrofani et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on HMMR function in spindle assembly.

claim: Aurora A can directly phosphorylate PLK1 on Thr210.
source: As Aurora A can directly phosphorylate PLK1 on Thr210 (Macůrek et al., 2008), our observed reduction in pPLK1(T210) in HMMR-silenced cells can be mechanistically explained through reduced Aurora A activity.
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on Aurora A function.

claim: The observed reduction in pPLK1(T210) in HMMR-silenced cells can be mechanistically explained through reduced Aurora A activity.
source: As Aurora A can directly phosphorylate PLK1 on Thr210 (Macůrek et al., 2008), our observed reduction in pPLK1(T210) in HMMR-silenced cells can be mechanistically explained through reduced Aurora A activity.
evidence: The manuscript draws this inference from published knowledge and observed data.

claim: Ran is a component of the centrosome proteome.
source: Ran is a component of the centrosome proteome (Andersen et al., 2003), although FRET-based assessment of Ran activity has not been seen at the centrosome (Kaláb et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites published proteomic data.

claim: FRET-based assessment of Ran activity has not been seen at the centrosome.
source: Ran is a component of the centrosome proteome (Andersen et al., 2003), although FRET-based assessment of Ran activity has not been seen at the centrosome (Kaláb et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on Ran activity measurements.

claim: HMMR appears dispensable for the Ran-GTP gradient generated at chromosomes.
source: However, HMMR appears dispensable for the Ran-GTP gradient generated at chromosomes, which strips NuMA and DHC-GFP at the midzone cortical region (Kiyomitsu and Cheeseman, 2012).
evidence: The data from Figures 4F-G support this conclusion.

claim: pHMMR has a spatially restricted role in the localization of Ran-GTP at centrosomes and spindle fibers downstream of PLK1 activity.
source: Therefore, our data supports a spatially restricted role for pHMMR in the localization of Ran-GTP at centrosomes and spindle fibers downstream of PLK1 activity.
evidence: The data from Figures 6 and 8 support this conclusion.

claim: The loss of spindle positioning in HMMR-silenced and HMMR-deleted or mutated cells and tissues, the occurrence of pleiotropic phenotypes in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a and Hmmrm/m mice, and the requirement of HMMR during meiotic and mitotic spindle assembly together indicate that the physiological function for HMMR is as a homeostasis, meiosis, and mitosis regulator.
source: Taken together, the results of our study identify HMMR as a key component of the PLK1-dependent mitotic spindle positioning pathway that is needed for neural development and neonatal survival. We suggest that the loss of spindle positioning identified here, and by others (Dunsch et al., 2012; Li et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015) (Li et al., 2017), in HMMR-silenced and HMMR-deleted or mutated cells and tissues, the occurrence of pleiotropic phenotypes observed in Hmmrtm1a/tm1a and Hmmrm/m mice, and the requirement of HMMR during meiotic (Groen et al., 2004; Joukov et al., 2006; Scrofani et al., 2015) and mitotic spindle assembly (Maxwell et al., 2005; Maxwell et al., 2003; Dunsch et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2014) together indicate that the physiological function for HMMR is as a homeostasis, meiosis, and mitosis regulator.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes multiple observations and published data to draw this conclusion.
